**Driving question:** how does extra workload or a setting change affect performance, CPU temperature and measured energy use?

## First, explore

Run an approved lightweight game and record the experience: graphics settings, perceived smoothness, resolution, controls and whether the computer was responsive. This is the engagement phase, not yet a controlled experiment.

## Then design a repeatable test

Choose a measurable outcome, such as a benchmark completion time, numerical throughput or available frame rate from a reproducible scene. Define the test duration, settings, machine model, room conditions and sampling interval.

- Run an idle baseline and at least three workload levels or comparable settings.
- Repeat each condition when possible.
- Record performance and CPU temperature from a **validated** sensor.
- If energy/power data are supported, label exactly what was measured: CPU package, a sensor-defined subsystem or entire wall outlet.
- Leave watts unavailable if you only have CPU utilization.
- Stop immediately for abnormal heat, failed cooling or other unsafe machine behavior.

A game can be an initial motivator. A controlled benchmark or fixed workload often gives more consistent numerical comparisons.

## Sample recording structure

| Condition | Trial | Temperature (C) | Performance measure | Power (W), if valid |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Idle | 1 | Record | Not applicable | Optional |
| Low | 1 | Record | Record | Optional |
| Medium | 1 | Record | Record | Optional |
| High | 1 | Record | Record | Optional |

Do not insert invented example measurements into final results.

## Questions to answer

What increased? What saturated? Did the temperature stabilize or continue rising? Are two computers fairly comparable? Is one configuration a reasonable compromise between performance and heat/energy?

**Evidence:** settings, raw CSV, repeat runs, one graph and a sentence about test limitations.
